workflows:
  version: 2
  ci-pipeline:
    jobs:
      - build
      
      # These jobs run in parallel after build
      - test-unit:
          requires:
            - build
      
      - test-integration:
          requires:
            - build
      
      - lint:
          requires:
            - build
      
      - security-scan:
          requires:
            - build
      
      # Deploy only after all parallel jobs succeed
      - deploy-staging:
          requires:
            - test-unit
            - test-integration
            - lint
            - security-scan
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

content.value:
Branching strategy determines how teams organize code contributions, merge changes, and maintain stability. CI pipelines are designed differently based on whether the team uses trunk-based, GitFlow, or feature branching.

Your branching strategy affects:
- How frequently code is integrated
- How complex merges become
- How CI pipelines are triggered
- How releases are managed
- How hotfixes are handled

Choosing the right strategy for your team's size, release cadence, and risk tolerance is essential for successful CI adoption.

items.definition: Everyone commits to main (or trunk) frequently, often multiple times per day. Feature flags hide incomplete work. Short-lived branches (hours, not days) are used for pairing or complex changes. This is the purest form of CI and enables the fastest feedback.

Each feature is developed in a dedicated branch. CI runs on the branch, and the branch is merged to main only after all tests pass and code review is complete. Branches typically last days to weeks. This is common in GitHub Flow.

A comprehensive branching model with main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches. Separates development work from release preparation. Suitable for large enterprises with scheduled releases. Can be heavy for CI because of long-lived branches.

Simpler than GitFlow: main branch is always deployable. Feature branches are created from main, and pull requests are used for review. After merging, deploy immediately. Popular for web applications and continuous delivery.
Combines feature branching with environment branches (staging, production). Uses merge requests and environments to manage deployments. Good for teams needing multiple deployment targets.

Contributors fork the main repository, make changes in their fork, and submit pull requests. Popular in open-source where contributors don't have write access to the main repo. CI runs on forks before PRs are merged.

content.title: 6.3 CI Pipeline Design for Each Strategy

content.value: Different branching strategies require different CI pipeline designs:

items.definition: Pipeline runs on every commit to main. Must be extremely fast (under 10 minutes) because commits are frequent. Feature flags hide incomplete work. If main breaks, fix it immediately.
Pipeline runs on every push to any branch. May include additional steps like code coverage comparison and preview deployments. After merging, pipeline deploys to staging/production.
Multiple pipelines: one for feature branches, one for develop branch, one for release branches, and one for main. Release branches may trigger additional acceptance tests.
CI runs on forks but may have limited access to secrets for security. After PR is merged, a separate pipeline runs with full permissions.

content.caption: CI Pipeline for Feature Branch Strategy
content.code:
name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches-ignore:
      - 'release/*'
      - 'main'
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  # Run on every push to any branch
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      
  # Run only on PRs to main
  pr-validation:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # Need full history for comparison
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Check test coverage against main
        run: |
          npm run test:coverage -- --changedSince=main
      - name: Build preview
        run: npm run build
      - name: Deploy preview to Vercel
        run: npx vercel --token ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}

---
# Pipeline for main branch (deploy)
name: Deploy Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Build and deploy
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run build
          npm run deploy:staging
  
  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: npm run deploy:production

content.title: 7. CI Configuration Files and Pipeline as Code
7.1 The Evolution of Pipeline as Code

content.value:
In the early days of CI, pipelines were configured through web UIs. Clicking through forms to set up builds was error-prone, unrepeatable, and impossible to version. If a server crashed, all configuration was lost.

**Pipeline as Code** solves these problems by treating pipeline definitions as code:
- Stored in version control alongside application code
- Versioned and traceable
- Reviewable through pull requests
- Testable before deployment
- Repeatable across environments

Most modern CI platforms use declarative YAML, JSON, or DSL-based configuration. This shift has transformed CI from a separate operational concern to an integral part of the development process.

      - name: Checkout code

        with:

      - name: Run type checker

      - name: Run tests with coverage

      - name: SonarCloud Scan

content.title: Pipeline as Code Best Practices
items: ✅ **Keep pipelines modular** – Split complex pipelines into reusable components. Use YAML anchors, templates, or shared libraries.
✅ **Use environment variables and secrets management** – Never hardcode credentials. Use built-in secret management (GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI Variables, Jenkins Credentials).
✅ **Always version control CI configs** – Store pipeline definitions in the repository. This enables traceability and disaster recovery.
✅ **Lint and validate configs** – Use tools like `actionlint` for GitHub Actions or `gitlab-ci-local` to validate before committing.
✅ **Reuse templates across repositories** – Create reusable pipeline templates to maintain consistency across multiple projects.
✅ **Set timeouts** – Prevent runaway jobs with appropriate timeouts (e.g., 10-30 minutes per job).
✅ **Use caching wisely** – Cache dependencies but be careful with cache invalidation. Include checksums in cache keys.
✅ **Fail fast** – Design pipelines to fail early. Run the fastest, most critical tests first.
✅ **Make pipelines self-documenting** – Use descriptive stage names and add comments for complex steps.
✅ **Test pipeline changes** – Run pipelines in a test branch before merging to main.
✅ **Monitor pipeline performance** – Track build times, cache hit rates, and failure rates. Optimize regularly.

content.caption: Example Following Best Practices
content.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml - Following Best Practices
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

# Set reasonable permissions
permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write
  pull-requests: write

# Reusable environment variables
env:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  BUILD_CACHE_KEY: build-${{ github.sha }}
  
# Concurrency control - cancel in-progress jobs on new push
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Validate and Lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5  # Fail fast if stuck
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
        
      - name: Lint code
        run: npm run lint
        
      - name: Type check
        run: npm run type-check

  test:
    name: Test (Node ${{ matrix.node-version }} on ${{ matrix.os }})
    needs: validate
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 10
    
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false  # Don't cancel all jobs if one fails
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node-version: [16.x, 18.x, 20.x]
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node-version: 16.x  # Skip incompatible combination
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
        
      - name: Upload test results
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        if: always()  # Upload even if tests fail
        with:
          name: test-results-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: junit.xml

  security:
    name: Security Scan
    needs: validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Run Snyk
        uses: snyk/actions/node@master
        continue-on-error: true  # Don't fail pipeline, just report
        env:
          SNYK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SNYK_TOKEN }}
        with:
          args: --severity-threshold=high
          
  coverage:
    name: Code Coverage
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Download all test results
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
      
      - name: Comment PR with coverage
        uses: actions/github-script@v6
        with:
          script: |
            const coverage = require('./coverage/coverage-summary.json');
            const message = `## Code Coverage Report\n\n`;
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: message
            });

  notify:
    name: Send Notifications
    needs: [test, security]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - name: Notify Slack on Success
        if: success()
        uses: 8398a7/action-slack@v3
        with:
          status: success
          fields: repo,message,commit,author,action,workflow
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}

      - name: Notify Slack on Failure
        if: failure()
        uses: 8398a7/action-slack@v3
        with:
          status: failure
          fields: repo,message,commit,author,action,workflow
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}

content.title: Single Server CI
content.explanation:
In centralized CI, one main server handles all builds and tests. This is the simplest architecture: a single Jenkins master, GitLab runner, or TeamCity server that executes all jobs.

**Advantages:**
- Simple to set up and maintain
- Single point of configuration
- Easy to monitor and manage
- No network complexity

**Disadvantages:**
- Single point of failure
- Can become a bottleneck for large teams
- Limited scalability
- All builds compete for the same resources

**Best For:** Small teams (5-15 developers), simple projects, or teams just starting with CI.

content.value:
Distributed CI farms spread builds across multiple machines. This architecture is essential for teams that need scalability, isolation, or specialized build environments.

**Key Components:**
- **Master/Coordinator** – Schedules jobs, manages queues, and aggregates results
- **Agents/Workers** – Execute individual build jobs
- **Shared Storage** – For artifacts and caches
- **Load Balancer** – Distributes work across agents

**Advantages:**
- Scales horizontally by adding more agents
- Isolated build environments prevent interference
- Can run builds on different platforms (Linux, Windows, macOS) in parallel
- No single point of failure with proper redundancy

**Disadvantages:**
- More complex to set up and maintain
- Requires network configuration
- May need shared storage solutions
- Higher infrastructure costs

**Best For:** Medium to large teams, projects with multiple platforms, organizations with many repositories.

content.title: Distributed CI Architecture
content.caption: Master node coordinates work across multiple agent nodes

content.value:
Cloud CI platforms (CircleCI, GitHub Actions, Travis CI, GitLab.com) provide elastic scaling, pay-as-you-go pricing, and minimal setup overhead. These services are ideal for modern SaaS and microservices architectures.

**Key Features:**
- **Elastic Scaling** – Automatically spins up resources as needed, scales to zero when idle
- **Managed Infrastructure** – No servers to patch, update, or maintain
- **Native Integrations** – Tight integration with version control, package registries, and cloud providers
- **Pay-per-use Pricing** – Costs align with actual usage
- **Global Availability** – Build agents in multiple regions

**Advantages:**
- Zero infrastructure maintenance
- Automatic updates and security patches
- Built-in high availability
- Massive parallelism
- Integrated with modern development tools

**Disadvantages:**
- Less control over infrastructure
- Potential vendor lock-in
- Costs can escalate with usage
- Compliance challenges for regulated industries

**Best For:** Startups, SaaS companies, open-source projects, teams wanting to focus on development rather than operations.

content.title: Combining On-Premises and Cloud
content.explanation:
Many enterprises use hybrid setups, combining on-prem agents for sensitive builds with cloud runners for scalability. This approach balances security, compliance, and performance.

**Common Hybrid Patterns:**

1. **Sensitive Code On-Premises** – Builds for proprietary code run on internal infrastructure; open-source dependencies and public projects use cloud runners.

2. **Secrets Management On-Premises** – Build agents access internal secrets vaults (HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk) without exposing them to the cloud.

3. **Compliance-Driven Isolation** – PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or SOC2 workloads run on dedicated on-prem hardware; non-sensitive builds use cloud for speed.

4. **Burst Capacity** – Use cloud agents during peak times while maintaining baseline capacity on-premises.

5. **Cross-Platform Testing** – Run Linux builds on cloud, Windows builds on-prem (or vice versa) based on cost and licensing.

**Implementation Approaches:**
- **Jenkins** with cloud plugins (Kubernetes, EC2) to spin up agents dynamically
- **GitLab** with hybrid runners (some on-prem, some cloud)
- **Custom solutions** using CI APIs to route jobs based on tags or labels

content.title: Case Study: Enterprise Hybrid CI at Global Bank
content.scenario: A global bank with 500+ developers needed to balance security requirements with development speed.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Strict regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, SOX) for financial applications
- 200+ microservices with frequent updates
- Need for fast feedback while maintaining security
- Limited on-prem infrastructure capacity

**The Hybrid Solution:**
1. **Tiered Pipeline Architecture**
   - Tier 1 (Fast feedback): Cloud runners for linting, unit tests, and builds
   - Tier 2 (Integration): On-prem runners for integration tests with internal systems
   - Tier 3 (Compliance): Air-gapped runners for security scans and compliance checks

2. **Smart Job Routing**
   - Jobs tagged with `security-level: low` run in cloud
   - Jobs tagged with `security-level: high` run on-prem
   - Special `data-sensitive` tag routes to dedicated hardware

3. **Secret Management**
   - Cloud runners access only public/development secrets
   - Production secrets never leave on-prem infrastructure
   - HashiCorp Vault provides unified secrets access with policies

**Infrastructure Setup:**
```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml - Hybrid runner configuration
variables:
  CLOUD_RUNNER_TAG: "cloud-runner"
  ONPREM_RUNNER_TAG: "onprem-runner"
  SECURE_RUNNER_TAG: "secure-runner"

stages:
  - fast-feedback
  - integration
  - compliance

# Runs on cloud - fast feedback
lint-and-unit:
  stage: fast-feedback
  tags:
    - cloud-runner
  script:
    - npm run lint
    - npm run test:unit

# Runs on-prem - needs internal DB access
integration-tests:
  stage: integration
  tags:
    - onprem-runner
  script:
    - npm run test:integration
  environment:
    name: staging

# Runs in air-gapped environment - compliance
security-scan:
  stage: compliance
  tags:
    - secure-runner
  script:
    - npm audit
    - snyk test
  artifacts:
    reports:
      security: gl-security-report.json
```

**Results:**
- Build times reduced by 60% (from 45 minutes to 18 minutes)
- 100% compliance with regulatory requirements
- Cloud costs optimized by 40% through tiered execution
- Developer satisfaction improved significantly

content.title: Docker and Kubernetes in CI
content.explanation:
Containers have revolutionized CI by providing consistent, reproducible, and isolated build environments. Every build can run in a fresh container, eliminating environment drift and 'works on my machine' problems.

**Benefits of Container-Based CI:**
- **Environment Consistency** – The same container image runs locally, in CI, and in production
- **Isolation** – Each build runs in its own container, preventing interference
- **Reproducibility** – Builds are deterministic; the same commit produces the same result
- **Caching** – Docker layer caching speeds up subsequent builds
- **Parallelism** – Easily spin up multiple containers for parallel test execution
- **Cleanup** – Containers are destroyed after use, leaving no residue

**Container CI Patterns:**

1. **Single Container Builds** – All build steps run in one container
   ```dockerfile
   FROM node:18
   WORKDIR /app
   COPY package*.json ./
   RUN npm ci
   COPY . .
   RUN npm test
   RUN npm run build
   ```

2. **Multi-Stage Builds** – Separate build and runtime stages
   ```dockerfile
   # Build stage
   FROM node:18 AS builder
   WORKDIR /app
   COPY package*.json ./
   RUN npm ci
   COPY . .
   RUN npm run build

   # Runtime stage
   FROM nginx:alpine
   COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
   ```

3. **Service Containers** – Spin up databases, message queues for integration tests
   ```yaml
   services:
     postgres:
       image: postgres:15
       env:
         POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
     redis:
       image: redis:7
   ```

4. **Kubernetes-native CI** – Each build runs as a Kubernetes pod with ephemeral volumes
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   spec:
     containers:
     - name: build
       image: node:18
       command: ["npm", "test"]
     - name: database
       image: postgres:15
   ```

content.caption: Container-Based CI with Docker Compose
content.code:
name: Container CI

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    # Service containers for integration tests
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:15
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
          POSTGRES_USER: testuser
          POSTGRES_DB: testdb
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
      
      redis:
        image: redis:7
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 6379:6379
      
      rabbitmq:
        image: rabbitmq:3-management
        ports:
          - 5672:5672
          - 15672:15672
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      
      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-
      
      - name: Build test container
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          tags: myapp:test
          cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
          cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache-new,mode=max
      
      - name: Run tests in container
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            --network host \
            -e DATABASE_URL=postgresql://testuser:testpass@localhost:5432/testdb \
            -e REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379 \
            -e RABBITMQ_URL=amqp://localhost:5672 \
            myapp:test npm run test:all
      
      - name: Build production image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:latest
            ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:${{ github.sha }}

  kubernetes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Set up kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
      
      - name: Set up kubeconfig
        run: |
          mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
          echo "${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG }}" > $HOME/.kube/config
      
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/myapp \
            myapp=${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/myapp:${{ github.sha }} \
            --record
          kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

**Tool Selection Criteria:**

content.title: Jenkins Deep Dive
content.explanation:
Jenkins is the most widely used open-source CI/CD automation server. With over 1,800 plugins, it can integrate with virtually any tool in the software delivery ecosystem.

**Key Features:**
- **Plugin-based Extensibility** – Plugins for version control, build tools, test frameworks, notifications, and deployment
- **Pipeline as Code** – Declarative and scripted pipelines (Jenkinsfile)
- **Distributed Builds** – Master/agent architecture for scaling
- **Rich Ecosystem** – Thousands of community-contributed plugins
- **Extensive API** – REST API for integration with other tools
- **Free and Open Source** – No licensing costs

**Architecture:**
- **Jenkins Master** – Manages jobs, schedules builds, serves UI
- **Jenkins Agents** – Execute build jobs (can be on-premises or cloud)
- **Shared Workspace** – Optional shared storage for artifacts

**Common Plugins:**
- Git, GitHub, GitLab – Source control integration
- Maven, Gradle, npm – Build tool integration
- JUnit, TestNG – Test reporting
- SonarQube – Code quality
- Docker, Kubernetes – Container builds
- Slack, Email – Notifications
- Blue Ocean – Modern UI

content.title: GitLab CI/CD Deep Dive
content.explanation:
GitLab CI/CD is integrated directly into GitLab's version control platform. Pipelines are defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml` files, making CI/CD part of the repository.

**Key Features:**
- **Single Application** – Source control, CI/CD, and container registry in one platform
- **Auto DevOps** – Automatic pipeline configuration for common languages
- **Review Apps** – Automatic deployment of preview environments for each MR
- **Built-in Container Registry** – Store Docker images alongside code
- **Kubernetes Integration** – Native deployment to Kubernetes clusters
- **Security Scanning** – Built-in SAST, DAST, dependency scanning
- **Pages** – Host static websites from CI artifacts

**Architecture:**
- **GitLab Instance** – Hosts repositories and CI/CD configuration
- **GitLab Runners** – Execute jobs (can be shared, group, or project-specific)
- **Runner Managers** – Coordinate multiple runners in Kubernetes or Docker

**Runner Types:**
- **Shared Runners** – Provided by GitLab.com or shared across projects
- **Group Runners** – Available to all projects in a group
- **Specific Runners** – Dedicated to a single project
- **Docker Runners** – Execute jobs in Docker containers
- **Kubernetes Runners** – Run jobs as Kubernetes pods
- **SSH Runners** – Execute jobs on remote machines

content.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml - Advanced Configuration

# Define stages
stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - security
  - package
  - review
  - staging
  - production
  - performance

# Global variables
variables:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2
  DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ''
  CACHE_FALLBACK_KEY: main
  
# Cache configuration
cache:
  key:
    files:
      - package-lock.json
  paths:
    - node_modules/
    - .npm/
  policy: pull-push

# Default configuration for all jobs
default:
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  before_script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
  interruptible: true
  timeout: 30m

# Include external templates
include:
  - template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Security/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Security/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml
  - project: 'my-group/shared-pipelines'
    file: '/deploy-templates.yml'
    ref: v1.2.3

# Lint job
lint:
  stage: lint
  script:
    - npm run lint
    - npm run format:check
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

# Parallel test matrix
test:
  stage: test
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - TEST_SUITE: [unit, integration, e2e]
        NODE_VERSION: [16, 18, 20]
  script:
    - npm run test:${TEST_SUITE}
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
    paths:
      - coverage/
      - cypress/screenshots/
    expire_in: 1 week

# Build job with caching
build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm run build
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

# Security scanning
security:
  stage: security
  script:
    - npm audit --production
    - snyk test
  allow_failure: true
  artifacts:
    reports:
      security: gl-security-report.json

# Package Docker image
package:
  stage: package
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind
  script:
    - docker build -t $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .
    - docker tag $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      exists:
        - Dockerfile

# Review app - temporary environment for MRs
review:
  stage: review
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X POST https://api.vercel.com/deploy
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://review-$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.example.com
    on_stop: stop_review
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'

stop_review:
  stage: review
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X DELETE https://api.vercel.com/deploy
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    action: stop
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'
      when: manual

# Deploy to staging
deploy-staging:
  stage: staging
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - chmod +x deploy.sh
    - ./deploy.sh staging
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://staging.example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

# Performance testing
performance:
  stage: performance
  image: grafana/k6
  script:
    - k6 run performance-tests.js
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - performance-report.html
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      changes:
        - performance-tests.js
        - src/**/*.js

# Deploy to production (manual gate)
deploy-production:
  stage: production
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh production
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  when: manual
  needs:
    - job: performance
      optional: true

# Post-deployment validation
post-deploy:
  stage: production
  script:
    - npm run test:smoke -- --url=https://example.com
  needs:
    - deploy-production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG

# Notifications
slack-notify:
  stage: .post
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' --data '{"text":"Pipeline $CI_PIPELINE_STATUS for $CI_PROJECT_NAME"}' $SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  when: always

content.title: GitHub Actions Deep Dive
content.explanation:
GitHub Actions integrates CI/CD directly into GitHub repositories. Workflows are defined in YAML and triggered by repository events (push, PR, release).

**Key Features:**
- **Event-Driven** – Trigger on any GitHub event (push, PR, issue comment, release)
- **Marketplace** – Thousands of pre-built actions for common tasks
- **Matrix Builds** – Test across multiple OSes, languages, and versions
- **Self-Hosted Runners** – Run actions on your own infrastructure
- **Environment Protection** – Manual approvals and environment variables
- **Secrets Management** – Encrypted secrets at organization and repository level
- **Artifacts** – Store and share build outputs
- **Packages** – Integrated container and package registry

**Architecture:**
- **Workflow** – YAML file defining automation
- **Job** – Collection of steps running on same runner
- **Step** – Individual task (run script or action)
- **Runner** – Server that executes jobs (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted)
- **Action** – Reusable unit of code (like a function)

**Runner Types:**
- **GitHub-hosted** – Ubuntu, Windows, macOS (free for public repos)
- **Self-hosted** – Run on your infrastructure (more control, free)
- **Larger Runners** – Premium runners with more CPU/RAM
- **GPU Runners** – For ML/AI workloads

content.caption: Advanced GitHub Actions Workflow
content.code:
name: Advanced CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
    tags: ['v*']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: 'Deployment environment'
        required: true
        default: 'staging'
        type: choice
        options:
          - staging
          - production

# Concurrency control
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# Environment variables
env:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  PNPM_VERSION: '8'
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  # Security scan job
  security:
    name: Security Scan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v2
        with:
          languages: javascript
      
      - name: Perform CodeQL Analysis
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v2
      
      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          scan-type: 'fs'
          scan-ref: '.'
          format: 'sarif'
          output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
      
      - name: Upload Trivy results to GitHub Security
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2
        with:
          sarif_file: 'trivy-results.sarif'

  # Build and test matrix
  build:
    name: Build and Test
    needs: security
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node-version: [16.x, 18.x, 20.x]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node-version: 18.x
            coverage: true
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node-version: 16.x
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      
      - name: Setup pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v2
        with:
          version: ${{ env.PNPM_VERSION }}
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'pnpm'
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install
      
      - name: Lint
        run: pnpm lint
      
      - name: Type check
        run: pnpm type-check
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: pnpm test -- --coverage
      
      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        if: matrix.coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: ./coverage/lcov.info
          flags: unittests
      
      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: test-results-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: |
            junit.xml
            coverage/

  # Build Docker image
  docker:
    name: Build Docker Image
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      
      - name: Extract metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v4
        with:
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}}
            type=sha,format=long
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}
      
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  # Deploy to environments
  deploy:
    name: Deploy to ${{ inputs.environment || 'staging' }}
    needs: docker
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.event_name == 'release'
    environment:
      name: ${{ github.event_name == 'release' && 'production' || 'staging' }}
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v2
        if: env.ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG != 'true'
        with:
          aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      
      - name: Deploy to ECS
        id: deploy
        run: |
          aws ecs update-service --cluster myapp --service ${{ env.ENVIRONMENT }} --force-new-deployment
          echo "url=https://${{ env.ENVIRONMENT }}.example.com" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
        env:
          ENVIRONMENT: ${{ github.event_name == 'release' && 'production' || 'staging' }}

  # Smoke tests
  smoke:
    name: Smoke Tests
    needs: deploy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run smoke tests
        run: |
          npx wait-on https://${{ needs.deploy.outputs.url }}
          npm run test:smoke -- --url=https://${{ needs.deploy.outputs.url }}

  # Performance tests
  performance:
    name: Performance Tests
    needs: deploy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'release'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run k6 tests
        uses: grafana/k6-action@v0.3.0
        with:
          filename: performance-tests.js
          flags: --vus 10 --duration 30s

  # Notifications
  notify:
    name: Send Notifications
    needs: [build, security, smoke]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Notify Slack
        uses: 8398a7/action-slack@v3
        with:
          status: ${{ job.status }}
          fields: repo,message,commit,author,action,workflow
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}

content.title: 10.1 The Role of Testing in CI
Testing is the Heart of CI
content.explanation:
Testing is the heartbeat of Continuous Integration. Without automated tests, CI pipelines are just automated build systems—they confirm that code compiles, but not that it works correctly.

The combination of unit, integration, system, performance, and security testing ensures that every change is validated quickly and reliably. A CI pipeline without comprehensive testing provides false confidence and can actually accelerate the delivery of defective software.

The Test Pyramid in CI follows a layered structure:

Top Layer – End-to-End (E2E) Tests:
Few in number, slow to execute, and more brittle. These validate complete user journeys and should focus only on critical business paths.

Middle Layer – Integration Tests:
Moderate in number and execution speed. These verify interactions between components, services, databases, and APIs.

Base Layer – Unit Tests:
High in number, fast, and reliable. These test individual functions or classes in isolation and should form 70–80% of the total test suite.

A healthy CI pipeline relies heavily on fast unit tests, supported by targeted integration tests and a minimal set of E2E tests. This structure ensures rapid feedback while maintaining confidence in system stability.

content.title: 10.2 Types of Tests in CI Pipelines

items.definition: Validate individual functions, methods, or classes in isolation. Mock all dependencies. Should run in milliseconds. Tools: JUnit, NUnit, pytest, Jest, Mocha.

Verify that components work together correctly. May use real databases, file systems, or external services. Slower than unit tests but catch interface issues. Tools: TestContainers, SpringBootTest, Docker Compose.
Test a component in isolation with its dependencies stubbed. Broader than unit tests but narrower than integration tests. Tools: WireMock, MockServer.
Verify that service providers and consumers agree on API contracts. Essential for microservices. Tools: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract.
Test complete user journeys through the entire application stack. Slowest and most brittle. Focus on critical paths. Tools: Selenium, Cypress, Playwright, TestCafe.
Validate that the software meets business requirements. Often written in business-readable formats (Gherkin). Tools: Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave.
Measure system speed, scalability, and resource usage under load. Run less frequently due to time/resource requirements. Tools: k6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust.
Identify vulnerabilities in code, dependencies, and configuration. Tools: SAST (SonarQube, CodeQL), DAST (OWASP ZAP), dependency scanning (Snyk, Dependabot).
Evaluate test quality by introducing small changes (mutations) to code and seeing if tests catch them. Tools: Stryker, PIT.
Quick sanity checks after deployment to verify basic functionality. Fast subset of E2E tests. Run after every deployment.
Ensure new changes haven't broken existing functionality. Often a combination of unit, integration, and E2E tests.
Detect unintended visual changes in UI. Compare screenshots against baselines. Tools: Percy, Applitools, Chromatic.

content.title: Optimizing Test Execution in CI
content.explanation:
As test suites grow, execution time becomes a critical concern. Slow tests delay feedback and reduce developer productivity. Here are strategies to keep tests fast while maintaining coverage:

**1. Test Parallelization**
Split tests across multiple machines or containers. Most CI tools support parallel test execution:
- GitHub Actions: `strategy.matrix`
- GitLab CI: `parallel` keyword
- Jenkins: Parallel stages
- CircleCI: Test splitting with `circleci tests split`

**2. Test Impact Analysis**
Run only tests that cover changed code. Tools like Bazel, Nx, and Turborepo analyze dependencies to determine which tests need to run.

**3. Test Sharding**
Divide tests into groups and run each group in parallel. Tools like Jest, pytest, and JUnit support sharding.

**4. Test Prioritization**
Run critical tests first (smoke tests, unit tests), then longer-running tests. Fail fast to save resources.

**5. Test Caching**
Cache test results to avoid re-running unchanged tests. Tools like Jest have built-in caching; CI systems can cache test outputs.

**6. Flaky Test Management**
Flaky tests (tests that sometimes pass, sometimes fail) undermine trust. Identify, quarantine, and fix them aggressively.

**7. Test Containerization**
Run tests in containers for consistent environments and easy parallelization.

**8. Database State Management**
Reset database state between tests. Use transactions, Docker snapshots, or tools like TestContainers.

content.title: Managing Test Data for Reliable Pipelines
content.explanation:
Reliable test data is essential for reproducible builds. In CI pipelines, teams need strategies to ensure tests run with consistent, predictable data.

**Challenges with Test Data in CI:**
- Databases start empty or with inconsistent state
- External APIs may be unavailable or rate-limited
- Sensitive production data cannot be used
- Tests may interfere with each other when run in parallel

**Test Data Strategies:**

1. **In-Memory Databases** – Use H2, SQLite, or other in-memory databases for fast, isolated tests.

2. **Database Snapshots** – Restore a known database state before tests. Tools like TestContainers, Docker, or Flyway can manage this.

3. **Transactional Tests** – Run each test in a transaction and roll back after completion.

4. **Factory/Builder Patterns** – Generate test data programmatically using factories (e.g., Factory Bot for Ruby, Factory Boy for Python).

5. **Seed Scripts** – Maintain scripts that populate databases with consistent seed data.

6. **Masked Production Data** – Use anonymized subsets of production data for realistic testing while protecting privacy.

7. **API Stubs/Mocks** – Use tools like WireMock, Mountebank, or MockServer to simulate external APIs.

8. **Service Virtualization** – Virtualize entire dependent services for integration testing.

9. **Parallel Test Isolation** – Use unique schemas or namespaces for parallel test runs to prevent interference.

content.title: Measuring Pipeline Health and Effectiveness
content.explanation:
Metrics ensure that CI pipelines deliver business value. Without measurement, you can't improve. Here are critical KPIs to track and optimize.

**Why Measure CI Metrics?**
- Identify bottlenecks and inefficiencies
- Track progress over time
- Justify investments in tooling and infrastructure
- Build a data-driven culture
- Alert when pipelines degrade

**Key Categories of CI Metrics:**
1. **Speed Metrics** – How fast is feedback?
2. **Reliability Metrics** – How trustworthy is the pipeline?
3. **Quality Metrics** – How effective is testing?
4. **Productivity Metrics** – How much value is delivered?
5. **Adoption Metrics** – How well is CI practiced?

content.title: Comprehensive CI Metrics Dashboard
rows: Percentage of builds that pass all stages
Indicates pipeline stability. Low success rate means flaky tests or unstable code.
Average time from commit to failure detection
Shorter MTTD means faster feedback. Developers can fix issues while context is fresh.
Average time to fix a broken build
Reflects team responsiveness and code complexity. Long MTTR indicates process problems.
Long builds discourage frequent commits and delay feedback.
Percentage of code exercised by tests
Shows testing thoroughness. Low coverage means higher risk of escaped defects.
Percentage of tests that fail intermittently
Flaky tests erode trust. Developers ignore failures if they're often false.
How often code is deployed to production
Higher frequency indicates agility and pipeline maturity.
Time from commit to production deployment
Measures end-to-end delivery speed. Long lead times delay value to customers.
Bugs found in production vs. testing
Shows testing effectiveness. High escape rate indicates test coverage gaps.
Time builds wait for available runners
Long queues indicate insufficient capacity. Developers wait, lose context.
Percentage of builds using cached dependencies
High cache hits speed up builds and reduce resource costs.
Number of commits per day per developer
Measures CI adoption. Low frequency suggests developers aren't integrating regularly.
When in pipeline failures typically occur
Fast-failing pipelines save resources. Fail early, fail fast.
Time to run full test suite
Slow tests are often skipped. Invest in test optimization.
Monitor cost efficiency. Optimize parallelization and caching.

# ci_metrics_collector.py import requests import json import time from datetime import datetime, timedelta from collections import defaultdict import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np # Use a valid matplotlib style plt.style.use('ggplot') class CIMetricsCollector: def __init__(self, github_token, repo_owner, repo_name): self.github_token = github_token self.repo_owner = repo_owner self.repo_name = repo_name self.headers = { 'Authorization': f'token {github_token}', 'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json' } self.base_url = f'https://api.github.com/repos/{repo_owner}/{repo_name}' def collect_workflow_runs(self, days=30): """Collect workflow run data from GitHub Actions""" since = (datetime.now() - timedelta(days=days)).isoformat() url = f"{self.base_url}/actions/runs" params = { 'created': f'>{since}', 'per_page': 100 } all_runs = [] page = 1 while True: params['page'] = page try: response = requests.get(url, headers=self.headers, params=params) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() if not data.get('workflow_runs'): break all_runs.extend(data['workflow_runs']) # Check if there are more pages if 'next' not in response.links: break page += 1 except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e: print(f"Error collecting workflow runs: {e}") break return all_runs def calculate_metrics(self, runs): """Calculate CI metrics from workflow runs""" metrics = {} if not runs: return { 'build_success_rate': 0, 'avg_build_duration': 0, 'p95_build_duration': 0, 'failure_by_workflow': {}, 'daily_trends': {}, 'mttr': 0 } # Build success rate total_runs = len(runs) successful_runs = sum(1 for r in runs if r.get('conclusion') == 'success') metrics['build_success_rate'] = (successful_runs / total_runs * 100) if total_runs > 0 else 0 # Build duration durations = [] for run in runs: if run.get('run_started_at') and run.get('updated_at'): try: start = datetime.fromisoformat(run['run_started_at'].replace('Z', '+00:00')) end = datetime.fromisoformat(run['updated_at'].replace('Z', '+00:00')) duration = (end - start).total_seconds() / 60 # minutes durations.append(duration) except (ValueError, TypeError): continue metrics['avg_build_duration'] = sum(durations) / len(durations) if durations else 0 metrics['p95_build_duration'] = sorted(durations)[int(len(durations) * 0.95)] if len(durations) > 0 else 0 # Failure patterns failures = [r for r in runs if r.get('conclusion') in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']] failure_by_workflow = defaultdict(int) for f in failures: workflow_name = f.get('name', 'unknown') failure_by_workflow[workflow_name] += 1 metrics['failure_by_workflow'] = dict(failure_by_workflow) # Daily trends runs_by_day = defaultdict(lambda: {'total': 0, 'success': 0, 'failure': 0, 'pending': 0}) for run in runs: if run.get('run_started_at'): day = run['run_started_at'][:10] runs_by_day[day]['total'] += 1 conclusion = run.get('conclusion') if conclusion == 'success': runs_by_day[day]['success'] += 1 elif conclusion in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']: runs_by_day[day]['failure'] += 1 else: runs_by_day[day]['pending'] += 1 metrics['daily_trends'] = dict(runs_by_day) # MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) # Find consecutive failures followed by success mttr_values = [] current_failure_start = None sorted_runs = sorted(runs, key=lambda r: r.get('run_started_at', '')) for run in sorted_runs: conclusion = run.get('conclusion') run_start = run.get('run_started_at') if not run_start: continue if conclusion in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']: if not current_failure_start: try: current_failure_start = datetime.fromisoformat(run_start.replace('Z', '+00:00')) except (ValueError, TypeError): continue else: if current_failure_start: try: success_time = datetime.fromisoformat(run_start.replace('Z', '+00:00')) repair_time = (success_time - current_failure_start).total_seconds() / 3600 # hours if repair_time > 0: # Only add positive repair times mttr_values.append(repair_time) except (ValueError, TypeError): pass finally: current_failure_start = None metrics['mttr'] = sum(mttr_values) / len(mttr_values) if mttr_values else 0 return metrics def generate_dashboard(self, metrics): """Generate HTML dashboard with visualizations""" # Create DataFrame for trends if metrics['daily_trends']: trends_df = pd.DataFrame([ {'date': day, **stats} for day, stats in metrics['daily_trends'].items() ]) trends_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(trends_df['date']) trends_df['success_rate'] = (trends_df['success'] / trends_df['total'] * 100).fillna(0) trends_df = trends_df.sort_values('date') # Figure 1: Success Rate Trend fig1, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6)) ax1.plot(trends_df['date'], trends_df['success_rate'], marker='o', linewidth=2, markersize=8) ax1.set_title('Build Success Rate Trend', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold') ax1.set_xlabel('Date', fontsize=12) ax1.set_ylabel('Success Rate (%)', fontsize=12) ax1.axhline(y=95, color='g', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label='Target (95%)') ax1.axhline(y=90, color='orange', linestyle=':', linewidth=2, label='Warning (90%)') ax1.legend(fontsize=10) ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.xticks(rotation=45) plt.tight_layout() plt.savefig('metrics_success_rate.png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight') plt.close() # Figure 2: Build Duration Distribution if 'avg_build_duration' in metrics and metrics['avg_build_duration'] > 0: fig2, (ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6)) # Duration trend ax2.plot(trends_df['date'], trends_df['total'], marker='s', linewidth=2, color='blue') ax2.set_title('Daily Build Count', fontsize=14) ax2.set_xlabel('Date') ax2.set_ylabel('Number of Builds') ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3) # Success/Failure breakdown ax3.bar(trends_df['date'], trends_df['success'], label='Success', alpha=0.8, color='green') ax3.bar(trends_df['date'], trends_df['failure'], bottom=trends_df['success'], label='Failure', alpha=0.8, color='red') ax3.set_title('Daily Build Results', fontsize=14) ax3.set_xlabel('Date') ax3.set_ylabel('Number of Builds') ax3.legend() plt.xticks(rotation=45) plt.tight_layout() plt.savefig('metrics_duration.png', dpi=100, bbox_inches='tight') plt.close() # Generate HTML html = f""" CI Metrics Dashboard - {self.repo_owner}/{self.repo_name}

📊 CI Metrics Dashboard

Repository: {self.repo_owner}/{self.repo_name}

Generated: {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')}

{metrics['build_success_rate']:.1f}%
Build Success Rate
{metrics['avg_build_duration']:.1f} min
Average Build Duration
{metrics['p95_build_duration']:.1f} min
95th Percentile Duration
{metrics['mttr']:.1f} hours
Mean Time to Repair (MTTR)

📈 Success Rate Trend

📊 Build Activity

❌ Failure by Workflow

{''.join(f'' for wf, count in metrics['failure_by_workflow'].items())}
WorkflowFailures% of Total
{wf}{count}{(count/len([r for r in runs if r.get("conclusion") in ["failure", "cancelled", "timed_out"]]))*100:.1f}%
""" with open('ci_dashboard.html', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f: f.write(html) print("✅ Dashboard generated: ci_dashboard.html") return html def _color_code(self, value, good_threshold, warning_threshold): if value >= good_threshold: return 'good' elif value >= warning_threshold: return 'warning' else: return 'bad' # Usage if __name__ == '__main__': import sys # Check for command line arguments if len(sys.argv) > 3: token = sys.argv[1] owner = sys.argv[2] repo = sys.argv[3] days = int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 30 else: # Interactive mode token = input("Enter GitHub token: ") owner = input("Enter repository owner: ") repo = input("Enter repository name: ") days = int(input("Enter number of days to analyze (default 30): ") or "30") collector = CIMetricsCollector( github_token=token, repo_owner=owner, repo_name=repo ) print(f"📡 Collecting workflow runs from the last {days} days...") runs = collector.collect_workflow_runs(days=days) print(f"✅ Collected {len(runs)} workflow runs") print("📊 Calculating metrics...") metrics = collector.calculate_metrics(runs) print("🎨 Generating dashboard...") collector.generate_dashboard(metrics) print("\n📈 Summary:") print(f" - Success Rate: {metrics['build_success_rate']:.1f}%") print(f" - Avg Duration: {metrics['avg_build_duration']:.1f} minutes") print(f" - MTTR: {metrics['mttr']:.1f} hours") print(f" - Total Workflows: {len(metrics['failure_by_workflow'])}") # Save metrics to JSON with open('ci_metrics.json', 'w') as f: json.dump(metrics, f, indent=2, default=str) print("💾 Metrics saved to ci_metrics.json")

content.title: The Complete CI Best Practices Guide
items: ✅ **Commit Early, Commit Often** – Small, frequent changes are easier to integrate and debug. Aim for multiple commits per day. Each commit should be a logical, self-contained change.
✅ **Keep Builds Fast** – Aim for <10 minutes for the complete pipeline. Slow builds discourage frequent commits. Invest in parallelization, caching, and faster hardware.
✅ **Automate Everything** – From builds to tests to deployment validations. No manual steps in the pipeline. If it can be automated, automate it.
✅ **Fail Fast, Fix Fast** – Stop the line when the build breaks. Make fixing the build the highest priority task. No new work until the build is green.
✅ **Test in Production-like Environments** – Avoid 'works on my machine' issues. Use staging environments that mirror production. Containerization helps here.
✅ **Use Feature Flags** – Deploy code safely without exposing it to all users. This enables trunk-based development and continuous deployment.
✅ **Monitor Pipeline Health** – Metrics should be visible on dashboards. Track success rates, durations, and failure patterns. Act on negative trends.
✅ **Treat Pipeline as Code** – Store pipeline definitions in version control. Review pipeline changes like code changes. This enables traceability and disaster recovery.
✅ **Parallelize Tests** – Use containers/nodes to run tests concurrently. Split tests by category, runtime, or module. Matrix builds are your friend.
✅ **Secure the Pipeline** – Scan dependencies, secrets, and containers continuously. Use SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning tools. Never store secrets in code.
✅ **Cache Dependencies Wisely** – Cache npm, Maven, pip packages to speed up builds. Use checksum-based cache keys. Monitor cache hit rates.
✅ **Isolate Build Environments** – Use containers or VMs to ensure consistent environments. Avoid shared state between builds. Clean up after each run.
✅ **Maintain a Staging Environment** – Deploy to staging after successful CI. Run integration and acceptance tests there. Catch environment-specific issues.
✅ **Practice Blameless Post-Mortems** – When builds fail, focus on process, not people. Use retrospectives to improve the pipeline. Share learnings across teams.
✅ **Keep Dependencies Fresh** – Regularly update dependencies to avoid security vulnerabilities. Automate dependency updates with Dependabot or Renovate.
✅ **Monitor Test Flakiness** – Track flaky tests separately. Quarantine or fix them immediately. Flaky tests destroy trust in the pipeline.
✅ **Use Semantic Versioning** – Version artifacts meaningfully. This enables traceability and rollback. Automate versioning in the pipeline.
✅ **Document the Pipeline** – Keep documentation up to date. New team members should understand how the pipeline works. Pipeline as code helps, but comments matter.
✅ **Review Pipeline Performance** – Regularly audit build times and resource usage. Optimize slow stages. Remove unused steps. The pipeline is a product—maintain it.
✅ **Celebrate Green Builds** – Positive reinforcement matters. Acknowledge when the team keeps the build green. Make pipeline health a team achievement.

content.title: Common CI Anti-Patterns
items: ❌ **The 'Works on My Machine' Syndrome** – Developers don't run tests locally, rely on CI to catch failures. CI becomes a debugging tool, not a validation tool.
❌ **Long-Lived Feature Branches** – Branches lasting weeks or months. Integration becomes painful, and CI provides little value. Practice trunk-based development.
❌ **Ignoring Broken Builds** – Allowing builds to stay red for hours or days. This normalizes failure and erodes discipline. Fix builds immediately.
❌ **The 'Testing Phase' at the End** – Treating testing as a separate phase after development. CI should test continuously, not just at the end.
❌ **Flaky Tests Without Action** – Ignoring intermittent failures. Teams learn to distrust the pipeline. Fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately.
❌ **Overly Long Builds** – Pipelines taking hours to complete. Developers stop waiting for feedback. Invest in optimization aggressively.
❌ **Insufficient Test Coverage** – Low coverage gives false confidence. Tests that don't test anything are worse than no tests. Measure coverage meaningfully.
❌ **Hardcoded Secrets in Pipeline** – Storing credentials in pipeline configuration. This is a major security risk. Use secret management tools.
❌ **No Local Testing** – Developers rely entirely on CI to catch errors. This creates long feedback loops. Encourage local testing with pre-commit hooks.
❌ **Pipeline Sprawl** – Too many similar pipelines that are hard to maintain. Use templates, shared libraries, and reusable actions. Consolidate where possible.
❌ **Ignoring Infrastructure** – Treating CI infrastructure as an afterthought. Slow runners, full disks, network issues plague the team. Invest in robust infrastructure.
❌ **No Visibility** – Pipeline status hidden from the team. Dashboards not maintained. Make pipeline health visible to everyone, all the time.

content.title: Netflix's CI Journey
content.scenario: Netflix's CI/CD platform handles thousands of daily deployments across 1,000+ microservices. Their Spinnaker-based platform integrates with Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- 1,000+ microservices with independent release cycles
- Thousands of engineers committing daily
- Need for zero-downtime deployments
- Global infrastructure across multiple regions

**The Solution:**
1. **Spinnaker as CD Platform** – Netflix built Spinnaker (now open-source) to handle multi-cloud deployments
2. **Jenkins for CI** – Each service has its own Jenkins pipeline
3. **Automated Canary Analysis** – Machine learning detects performance regressions
4. **Chaos Engineering** – Automated chaos testing (Chaos Monkey) validates resilience

**Key Practices:**
- **Trunk-Based Development** – All developers commit to main, use feature flags
- **Automated Testing Pyramid** – Extensive unit tests, integration tests, and canary analysis
- **Immutable Infrastructure** – Every deployment creates new instances, no in-place updates
- **Real-Time Monitoring** – Metrics from every deployment feed back into CI decisions

**Results:**
- 4,000+ deployments per day
- 99.99% availability despite constant change
- Rollbacks in under 5 minutes when issues detected
- 80% reduction in deployment-related incidents

content.title: Google's Blaze/Bazel System
content.scenario: Google's monorepo contains billions of lines of code with thousands of daily commits. Their CI system must scale massively while maintaining fast feedback.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Single repository with all of Google's code
- 25,000+ engineers committing daily
- 50,000+ commits per day
- Build and test across multiple languages and platforms

**The Solution:**
1. **Bazel Build System** – Google built Blaze (open-sourced as Bazel) for hermetic, reproducible builds
2. **Distributed Build Execution** – Builds distributed across thousands of machines
3. **Test Impact Analysis** – Only tests affected by changes are run
4. **Remote Caching** – Build artifacts cached globally

**Key Technologies:**
- **Bazel** – Build and test with precise dependency analysis
- **RBE (Remote Build Execution)** – Distributed build farm
- **Test Scheduler** – Prioritizes and parallelizes test execution
- **Code Search & Cross-Reference** – Enables understanding across codebase

**Results:**
- 99% of builds complete in under 5 minutes
- Trillions of test cases executed daily
- 80% reduction in build time through caching
- Developers get feedback within minutes for most changes

content.title: Etsy's Deploy Culture
content.scenario: Etsy is known for rapid deployments (50+ per day). Their CI pipeline emphasizes fast rollback mechanisms and feature flagging to reduce risk.
content.details:
**The Culture:**
- 'Deploy whenever you want' philosophy
- Engineers own their code from commit to production
- Blameless post-mortems for incidents
- Metrics-driven decision making

**Key Practices:**
1. **Feature Flags** – New features hidden behind flags, enabled gradually
2. **Automated Testing** – Comprehensive test suite runs on every commit
3. **Deployinator** – Custom deployment tool with one-click rollback
4. **ChatOps** – Deployments triggered and monitored via chat
5. **Dark Launches** – Run new code in production without exposing to users

**Pipeline Design:**
- Commit triggers Jenkins build
- Unit tests run (2-3 minutes)
- Integration tests in staging (5 minutes)
- Canary deployment to 1% of servers
- Monitor metrics for 5 minutes
- Gradual rollout to remaining servers

**Results:**
- 50+ deployments per day
- Mean time to recovery under 10 minutes
- 90% of commits reach production within 24 hours
- Developer satisfaction consistently high

content.title: HIPAA-Compliant CI Pipeline
content.scenario: A healthcare SaaS company needed to maintain HIPAA compliance while accelerating development. They integrated TestRail with Jenkins, ensuring every regulatory compliance test runs before releases.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- HIPAA compliance requirements
- Sensitive patient data
- Audit trails for all changes
- 50+ regulated controls to verify

**The Solution:**
1. **TestRail Integration** – Manual test cases tracked in TestRail, triggered by Jenkins
2. **Automated Compliance Checks** – Scripts verify PHI handling, encryption, access controls
3. **Audit Logging** – Every CI action logged for compliance reviews
4. **Approval Gates** – Manual approvals required for production deployments

**Pipeline Stages:**
```
Commit → Build → Unit Tests → Integration Tests → 
Compliance Scan → Security Scan → Manual Approval → 
Staging Deploy → UAT Tests → Production Deploy
```

**Results:**
- 40% reduction in defect escape rate
- Compliance audit time reduced from 2 weeks to 2 days
- 100% traceability from commit to production
- Passed HIPAA audit with zero findings

content.title: Global Bank's DevSecOps Transformation
content.scenario: A global bank used CI pipelines with SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Zephyr for compliance. Build duration reduced from 4 hours to 30 minutes with containerized pipelines.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Strict regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, SOX)
- 200+ microservices with frequent updates
- Need for fast feedback while maintaining security
- Legacy build infrastructure (4+ hour builds)

**The Solution:**
1. **Containerized Builds** – Migrated from physical agents to Kubernetes
2. **Parallel Security Scanning** – SAST, DAST, and dependency scans run in parallel
3. **Test Impact Analysis** – Only run tests affected by changes
4. **Quality Gates** – Automatic failure if coverage drops or vulnerabilities found

**Security Integration:**
- **SAST** – Checkmarx scans for code vulnerabilities
- **DAST** – OWASP ZAP scans running applications
- **SCA** – Black Duck for dependency scanning
- **Secret Scanning** – TruffleHog detects secrets in code
- **Container Scanning** – Twistlock scans Docker images

**Results:**
- Build duration reduced from 4 hours to 30 minutes
- 95% of security issues caught before staging
- Zero critical security incidents in 2 years
- Developer productivity increased by 300%

content.title: Taming Flaky Tests
content.explanation:
Flaky tests are the #1 enemy of reliable CI pipelines. They undermine trust, waste time, and hide real failures. A comprehensive strategy is needed to manage them.

**What Makes Tests Flaky?**
- **Timing Issues** – Race conditions, async operations
- **Order Dependencies** – Tests that assume a specific order
- **External Dependencies** – Network calls, APIs, databases
- **Resource Leaks** – Memory, file handles, connections
- **Random Data** – Non-deterministic test data
- **Environment Differences** – Different OS, locale, timezone
- **Concurrency Issues** – Parallel test interference

**Flaky Test Management Strategy:**

1. **Detection**
   - Track test results over time
   - Flag tests that pass and fail on same code
   - Use tools like Test Analytics, Flaky Test Detector

2. **Quarantine**
   - Move flaky tests to separate suite
   - Don't block CI on quarantined tests
   - Track flakiness metrics

3. **Analysis**
   - Investigate root causes
   - Review test implementation
   - Look for timing, order, or data issues

4. **Fix or Delete**
   - Fix the test or the code
   - If can't fix, delete the test
   - Document decisions

5. **Prevention**
   - Code review guidelines for tests
   - Training on test design
   - Tools to prevent common flaky patterns

content.title: The Next Generation of CI
items: 🤖 **AI-Powered CI** – Machine learning models predict flaky tests, auto-optimize build parallelization, suggest fixes for failing builds, and prioritize test execution based on risk analysis.
📦 **GitOps Integration** – CI pipelines triggering GitOps-style deployments where infrastructure state is managed through Git. CI validates changes, GitOps applies them.
🔒 **Shift-Left Security (DevSecOps)** – Security integrated throughout the pipeline. SAST, DAST, SCA, and container scanning run automatically. Security gates at every stage.
⚡ **Serverless CI/CD** – Event-driven, scalable pipelines with zero infrastructure management. Pay only for what you use. Auto-scaling to handle peak loads.
🌍 **Edge CI/CD** – Deploying builds/tests closer to where users are. Testing at edge locations for latency-sensitive applications. CDN-based testing.
☁️ **Hybrid and Multi-Cloud CI** – Pipelines designed to span across cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure. Vendor-agnostic pipelines.
🎯 **Test Impact Analysis Everywhere** – AI-powered analysis of code changes to determine exactly which tests need to run. Eliminates unnecessary test execution.
🔄 **Self-Healing Pipelines** – Pipelines that automatically detect and recover from failures. Auto-retry flaky tests, provision new agents when nodes fail.
📊 **Unified Observability** – Metrics, logs, and traces from CI pipelines integrated with application monitoring. End-to-end visibility from commit to production.
🔧 **Pipeline as Product** – Treating CI pipelines as products with dedicated teams, roadmaps, and user feedback. Internal developer platforms for CI/CD.
🎨 **Low-Code/No-Code CI** – Visual pipeline builders for non-experts. Templates and wizards for common scenarios. Democratizing CI/CD.
🔐 **Supply Chain Security** – SBOM generation, dependency verification, signed commits, and attestations integrated into CI. Protecting software supply chains.
📈 **Predictive Analytics** – Predicting build failures before they happen. Identifying risky commits. Suggesting preventive actions.
🔄 **Continuous Feedback** – Pipelines that provide richer feedback: code suggestions, performance insights, security recommendations, all in the developer's workflow.
🌐 **Universal CI** – Single pipeline that works across any language, any platform, any cloud. No more re-inventing pipelines per project.

tutorials.title: 🚀 Continuous Delivery (CD)
tutorials.description: Master Continuous Delivery (CD) to ensure every code change is production-ready. Learn how to automate deployment pipelines, implement deployment strategies, and build a culture of reliable, frequent releases that deliver value to users faster and safer.

content.title: Defining Continuous Delivery
content.explanation:
Continuous Delivery (CD) is a software development practice where every code change is built, tested, and prepared for release to production. It extends Continuous Integration by ensuring that the software is always in a deployable state, enabling teams to release at any time with minimal manual effort.

At its core, CD is about **making deployments boring**. In traditional software delivery, deployments were rare, high-risk events that required extensive planning, late nights, and heroics. CD flips this model by making deployments frequent, automated, and routine—so routine that they become unremarkable.

**The CD Mindset:**
- Deployments should be low-risk and reversible
- Quality is built in, not tacked on at the end
- Feedback loops should be short and actionable
- Everyone shares responsibility for deliverability

**Key Distinctions:**
- **Continuous Delivery** – Code is always deployable, but may require manual approval for production
- **Continuous Deployment** – Every change that passes tests is automatically deployed to production

content.text: Continuous Delivery is the ability to get changes of all types—including new features, configuration changes, bug fixes and experiments—into production, or into the hands of users, safely and quickly in a sustainable way.

items.definition: Every commit results in a potentially shippable product. Teams should be able to deploy to production with a single click at any moment.
All steps from commit to deployment are automated—build, test, deploy, verify, and rollback if necessary.
Development, staging, and production environments are as similar as possible to prevent environment-specific issues.
Deployments follow the same process every time, eliminating manual steps that introduce variability and errors.
Metrics, logs, and monitoring provide immediate insight into the health of deployments and applications.
Security checks are automated throughout the pipeline, not performed as a final gate.

content.value:
**When to use each approach:**

- **CI only**: Teams just starting with automation, small projects, or when regulatory requirements don't permit frequent releases
- **Continuous Delivery**: Most teams—balances automation with control, allows business to decide release timing
- **Continuous Deployment**: SaaS companies, teams with high test coverage and confidence, when rapid iteration is critical

content.title: Why Organizations Invest in CD

**💰 Reduced Cost of Release** – Automated pipelines eliminate manual effort, reducing the cost of each release by 50-80%.
**🎯 Lower Risk** – Small, frequent changes are easier to validate and roll back. Failed deployments affect fewer users and are fixed faster.
**📊 Better Quality** – Automated testing catches defects early. Continuous feedback from users improves product-market fit.
**😊 Happier Teams** – No more late-night deployment marathons. Developers focus on features, not firefighting. Teams gain confidence and morale.
**🔒 Improved Security** – Security checks automated throughout the pipeline. Faster patching of vulnerabilities.
**📋 Regulatory Compliance** – Automated audit trails show exactly what changed, who approved it, and when it deployed.
**🚀 Innovation Velocity** – Experiment freely with feature flags and A/B testing. Learn from real user behavior and iterate quickly.

content.title: Understanding Pipeline Stages
content.explanation:
A CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that code passes through on its journey from commit to production. Each stage increases confidence that the software is safe to release. The pipeline acts as a factory assembly line for software, with quality checks at every step.

**Key characteristics of effective pipelines:**
- **Fast** – Feedback within minutes, not hours
- **Reliable** – Results are consistent and trustworthy
- **Repeatable** – Same commit produces same result every time
- **Visible** – Everyone can see status and logs
- **Safe** – Automatic rollback on failure
- **Auditable** – Complete trail of what, when, and who

# .gitlab-ci.yml - Complete CD Pipeline

stages:
  - commit

  - staging

  - production
  - verification

variables:
  DOCKER_REGISTRY: registry.gitlab.com
  DOCKER_IMAGE: $DOCKER_REGISTRY/$CI_PROJECT_PATH:$CI_COMMIT_SHA

# Cache dependencies for speed
cache:
  paths:
    - node_modules/
    - .npm/

# Stage 1: Commit Stage - Fast feedback
commit:
  stage: commit
  image: node:18
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint
    - npm run type-check
    - npm run test:unit -- --coverage
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
  coverage: '/All files[^|]*\|[^|]*(\d+\.\d+)/'

# Stage 2: Build and Package
build:
  stage: acceptance
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind
  script:
    - docker build -t $DOCKER_IMAGE .
    - docker tag $DOCKER_IMAGE $DOCKER_REGISTRY/$CI_PROJECT_PATH:latest
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $DOCKER_REGISTRY
    - docker push $DOCKER_IMAGE
    - docker push $DOCKER_REGISTRY/$CI_PROJECT_PATH:latest
  only:
    - main

# Stage 3: Acceptance Tests
acceptance:
  stage: acceptance
  image: node:18
  services:
    - postgres:15
    - redis:7
  variables:
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:testpass@postgres:5432/testdb

  script:

    - npm run test:integration
    - npm run test:api
  artifacts:
    when: always

# Stage 4: Deploy to Staging
deploy-staging:
  stage: staging
  image: alpine:latest
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - chmod +x deploy.sh

    url: https://staging.example.com
  only:

  image: node:18
  script:

  only:

# Stage 6: Manual Approval Gate
